title: What is the principle of least privilege — give users and services the MINIMUM permissions they need to do their job, not more?
topicTitle: Web Vulnerabilities — SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF

s1_definition.profdef: The principle of least privilege (PoLP) states that every user, service, process, and credential should be granted only the minimum permissions required to perform its function, and nothing more. It limits the blast radius of mistakes, bugs, and compromised accounts by ensuring a breached identity can only do the small set of things it was explicitly allowed. It applies across layers — application roles and scopes, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access — and is paired with time-bounding and just-in-time elevation for sensitive actions.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a teller's key opens only the teller drawer, not the vault, and a cleaner's pass opens only the lobby, not the server room. Nobody carries a master key "just in case." If a teller's key is stolen, the thief reaches only the teller drawer, not the whole bank. Least privilege is the bank handing each person and each machine exactly the keys their job needs and no more, so one lost key cannot open everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grant the minimum permission needed — so a compromise can do minimum damage.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The principle of least privilege (PoLP) states that every user, service, process, and credential should be granted only the minimum permissions required to perform its function, and nothing more. It limits the blast radius of mistakes, bugs, and compromised accounts by ensuring a breached identity can only do the small set of things it was explicitly allowed. It applies across layers — application roles and scopes, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access — and is paired with time-bounding and just-in-time elevation for sensitive actions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, a teller's key opens only the teller drawer, not the vault, and a cleaner's pass opens only the lobby, not the server room. Nobody carries a master key "just in case." If a teller's key is stolen, the thief reaches only the teller drawer, not the whole bank. Least privilege is the bank handing each person and each machine exactly the keys their job needs and no more, so one lost key cannot open everything.

**One line to remember:** Grant the minimum permission needed — so a compromise can do minimum damage.

sections.s2_technical:
At the application layer, least privilege means narrow roles and scopes. A reporting service gets a read-only scope like `account:read`, never `account:write`, and an OAuth2 token carries only the scopes consented to. In Spring Security this is enforced with `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_account:read')")`, so even if the service is tricked, it cannot move money because it never held the write authority.

At the database layer, the application user is granted only the statements it needs — for example SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE on specific tables, but not DROP or DELETE on everything, and definitely not superuser. At the cloud layer, IAM policies grant specific actions on specific resources rather than wildcard `*` permissions, and roles are assumed temporarily rather than using long-lived root credentials. At the OS layer, services run as non-root users with minimal file and network permissions.

The senior points: least privilege reduces the blast radius of both external attacks and internal mistakes, and it is reinforced by just-in-time, time-bounded elevation — grant an admin extra rights only for the minutes they need, then revoke. It pairs with separation of duties so no single identity can both initiate and approve a sensitive action. The common anti-patterns are wildcard permissions, shared admin accounts, and "temporary" broad grants that never get removed. Regular access reviews and automated detection of over-privileged identities keep privilege creep in check. In a bank, PoLP is often a regulatory requirement, not just good hygiene.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reporting service only needs to read balances for dashboards, but someone granted it full read-write access. If it is compromised, the attacker can move money. This is exactly a least-privilege violation — the service should hold read-only access.

Problem 2 — An admin needs elevated rights to unlock an account, but giving permanent admin rights means a stolen admin session is catastrophic forever. This is exactly why just-in-time, time-bounded elevation exists — grant the power briefly, then revoke.

Our mini-project builds a `PermissionService` that enforces scoped permissions and a time-bounded elevation grant. The demo shows a read-only service reading successfully but being blocked from writing, and an admin getting temporary elevation to unlock an account that expires afterward.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a reporting service granted only account:read, and an admin needing temporary account:unlock.

Step 1: The reporting service is granted account:read — the minimum it needs. When it calls checkPermission for account:read, a valid grant exists, so access is allowed.

Step 2: The same service calls checkPermission for account:write. No grant exists, and the system denies by default, so AccessDeniedException is thrown. Even a compromised reporting service cannot move money because it was never given write access.

Step 3: The admin needs to unlock an account, so they receive a time-bounded elevation for account:unlock valid for ten minutes. While valid, checkPermission allows the unlock. The powerful permission exists only briefly and only for the specific action.

Step 4: After the elevation expires (simulated), checkPermission for account:unlock finds no valid grant and denies. The admin is back to minimal rights, so a stolen admin session after the window cannot unlock accounts. Deny-by-default plus time-bounded elevation keeps privilege minimal at all times.

```text
2026-11-01 00:00:00.010 INFO    [LeastPrivilegeDemo] reporting-service read allowed (has account:read)
2026-11-01 00:00:00.012 SEVERE  [LeastPrivilegeDemo] reporting-service write blocked: reporting-service lacks permission: account:write
2026-11-01 00:00:00.013 INFO    [LeastPrivilegeDemo] admin-priya temporarily elevated -> unlock allowed
2026-11-01 00:00:00.014 WARNING [LeastPrivilegeDemo] admin-priya elevation expired: admin-priya lacks permission: account:unlock
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Principal requests action
    │
    ▼
  checkPermission(principal, permission)   [DENY BY DEFAULT]
    │
    ├─ valid grant exists? ──no──→ AccessDenied (403)
    │          │ yes
    ▼          ▼
  read-only svc: account:read          account:write (never granted)
  admin: account:unlock WHILE elevation valid
 AFTER elevation expires (time-bounded)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The principle of least privilege says that every user, service, process, and credential should be granted only the minimum permissions needed to do its job, and nothing more. Its purpose is to limit the blast radius: if an identity is compromised or makes a mistake, it can only affect the small set of things it was explicitly allowed to touch. It applies at every layer — application roles and scopes, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access.

In my banking project I apply it concretely. The reporting service only needs to read balances for dashboards, so it gets a read-only scope and nothing else; even if it is compromised, it cannot move money because it never held write access. At the database layer the application user is granted only the statements it needs and never superuser or broad DROP rights, and in the cloud we grant specific actions on specific resources rather than wildcard permissions and assume roles temporarily rather than using long-lived root credentials.

For sensitive actions I pair least privilege with just-in-time, time-bounded elevation. In my demo the read-only service reads successfully but is blocked by deny-by-default when it tries to write, and an admin receives a ten-minute elevation to unlock an account that automatically expires afterward, so a stolen admin session outside that window cannot do the privileged action.

The nuances I stress are separation of duties so no single identity can both initiate and approve a sensitive transfer, avoiding the classic anti-patterns of wildcard permissions, shared admin accounts, and temporary grants that never get removed, and running regular access reviews to catch privilege creep. In a bank this is not just good hygiene — it is frequently a regulatory requirement — and it is one of the cheapest, highest-impact controls for shrinking the damage any single compromise can cause.

keyPoints: SQL Injection: use parameterized queries, never concatenate user input
XSS: sanitize output, use Content-Security-Policy header
CSRF: use anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookie attribute
SSRF: validate/whitelist URLs, block internal network access
